bib.title: SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text

legacy_report:
SOURCE: SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. Pranav Rajpurkar, Jian Zhang, Konstantin Lopyrev, Percy Liang (Stanford). EMNLP 2016, pp. 2383–2392 (doi 10.18653/v1/d16-1264).
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/rajpurkar-2016-squad.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 10 of 10 pages, 37,267 of 37,267 characters, including the references. Page numbers below are PDF pages, with the proceedings page in brackets (PDF p1 = 2383).

CLAIMS (most important first)

- claim: EM and F1 definitions. Both metrics ignore punctuation and articles. EM counts a prediction as correct if it matches any reference exactly. F1 treats prediction and reference as bags of tokens, takes the maximum F1 over all references, then averages over questions (macro-averaged).
  number: none
  setup: model evaluation on SQuAD v1.0 dev and test.
  quote: "Both metrics ignore punctuations and articles (a, an, the). Exact match. This metric measures the percentage of predictions that match any one of the ground truth answers exactly. (Macro-averaged) F1 score. This metric measures the average overlap between the prediction and ground truth answer. We treat the prediction and ground truth as bags of tokens, and compute their F1. We take the maximum F1 over all of the ground truth answers for a given question, and then average over all of the questions."
  where: p7 [2389], §6.1. The paper gives no other normalisation: it does not mention lowercasing or whitespace handling. Do not attribute those to the paper.

- claim: Every dev and test question has at least 3 reference answers: the original plus at least 2 more. They were collected to estimate human performance and to make evaluation more robust.
  number: at least 2 additional, at least 3 total
  setup: second-pass workers saw the questions and paragraphs and were asked to pick the shortest answering span, or to submit with no answer if no span answered the question.
  quote: "To get an indication of human performance on SQuAD and to make our evaluation more robust, we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets." / "asked to select the shortest span in the paragraph that answered the question."
  where: p4 [2386], §3

- claim: Human performance was measured by treating the second answer as the prediction and the remaining answers as references. Most mismatches come from including or leaving out non-essential words, not from real disagreement.
  number: test 77.0% EM / 86.8% F1
  setup: SQuAD v1.0 test set.
  quote: "we treat the second answer to each question as the human prediction, and keep the other answers as ground truth answers. The resulting human performance score on the test set is 77.0% for the exact match metric, and 86.8% for F1. Mismatch occurs mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases (e.g., monsoon trough versus movement of the monsoon trough) rather than fundamental disagreements about the answer."
  where: p7 [2389], §6.2

- claim: Headline results (Table 5). Logistic regression beats the sliding-window baselines by a wide margin but stays far below humans: 51.0 vs 86.8 test F1, a gap of about 36 points.
  number: LR 40.0/40.4 EM and 51.0/51.0 F1 (dev/test); Human 80.3/77.0 EM and 90.5/86.8 F1; Sliding Window 13.2/12.5 EM and 20.2/19.7 F1; Sliding Window + Distance 13.3/13.0 EM and 20.2/20.0 F1; Random 1.1/1.3 EM and 4.1/4.3 F1
  setup: SQuAD v1.0 dev and test.
  quote: "Logistic Regression 40.0% 40.4% 51.0% 51.0% / Human 80.3% 77.0% 90.5% 86.8%"
  where: p8 [2390], Table 5

- claim: Within four months, neural models had more than halved the gap.
  number: 70.3% F1
  setup: Wang and Jiang (2016), on SQuAD v1.1. The authors say v1.0 results are similar.
  quote: "Wang and Jiang (2016) obtained 70.3% F1 on SQuAD v1.1 (results on v1.0 are similar). These results are still well behind human performance, which is 86.8% F1 based on inter-annotator agreement."
  where: p2 [2384]. Also p9: "the gap ... has more than halved"

- claim: Split by answer type, the model does best on dates and numbers and worst on phrases and clauses. Human scores are much more even across types.
  number: LR / Human dev F1: Date 72.1/93.9; Other Numeric 62.5/92.9; Person 56.2/95.4; Location 55.4/94.1; Other Entity 52.2/92.6; Common NP 46.5/88.3; Adjective Phrase 37.9/86.8; Verb Phrase 31.2/82.4; Clause 34.3/84.5; Other 34.8/86.1
  setup: dev set, logistic regression.
  quote: "Logistic regression performs better on certain types of answers, namely numbers and entities. On the other hand, human performance is more uniform." / "The model performs worst on other answer types, which together form 47.6% of the dataset."
  where: p8 [2390], Table 7

- claim: Model performance falls as the syntactic divergence between question and answer sentence grows. Human performance stays flat. The authors propose the size of this drop as a test of whether a model generalises the right way.
  number: none. The values appear only as a plot (Fig. 5), so none can be quoted.
  setup: dev F1, divergence 0–8.
  quote: "Interestingly, humans do not seem to be sensitive to syntactic divergence ... Measuring the degree of degradation could therefore be useful in determining the extent to which a model is generalizing in the right way."
  where: p9 [2391]

- claim: How syntactic divergence is computed. Find anchor words shared by question and sentence. Take the unlexicalised dependency path from the anchor to the wh-word in the question, and from the anchor to the answer span in the sentence. Divergence is the minimum edit distance (deletions and insertions) between these paths over all anchors. It ignores lexical variation.
  number: none
  quote: "The syntactic divergence is then defined as the minimum edit distance over all possible anchors." / "Note that our syntactic divergence ignores lexical variation. Also, small divergence does not mean that a question is easy"
  where: p5 [2387]

- claim: Answer-type mix, assigned automatically with CoreNLP parses, POS and NER tags.
  number: dates/numbers 19.8%; proper nouns 32.6%; common NPs 31.8%; other 15.8%
  quote: "dates and other numbers make up 19.8% of the data; 32.6% of the answers are proper nouns of three different types; 31.8% are common noun phrases answers; and the remaining 15.8% are made up of adjective phrases, verb phrases, clauses and other types."
  where: p4 [2386], Table 2

- claim: Reasoning types, hand-labelled on 192 dev examples (4 questions from each of 48 articles). Categories can overlap.
  number: syntactic variation 64.1%; synonymy 33.3%; multiple-sentence 13.6%; world knowledge 9.1%; ambiguous 6.1%
  quote: "We manually labeled 192 examples into one or more of the above categories."
  where: p5 [2387], Table 3

- claim: Dataset size and construction. 536 articles were sampled uniformly from the top 10,000 English Wikipedia articles by PageRank. Paragraphs under 500 characters were dropped, leaving 23,215 paragraphs. The split is 80/10/10 by article.
  number: 107,785 QA pairs, 536 articles
  quote: "SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles, and is almost two orders of magnitude larger than previous manually labeled RC datasets such as MCTest" / "We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%)."
  where: p2 [2384]; p3–4 [2385–6]

- claim: Crowd collection ran on Daemo, backed by Mechanical Turk. Workers needed a 97% HIT acceptance rate, at least 1,000 HITs, and to be in the US or Canada. They spent 4 minutes per paragraph at $9 per hour and wrote up to 5 questions per paragraph, highlighting each answer. Copying was discouraged with a reminder prompt and by disabling copy-paste. The second-pass pace was 5 questions per 2 minutes.
  number: $9/hr; 4 min/paragraph; up to 5 questions
  quote: "Workers were asked to spend 4 minutes on every paragraph, and paid $9 per hour for the number of hours required to complete the article." / "crowdworkers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words, without copying word phrases from the paragraph. On the interface, this was reinforced by a reminder prompt at the beginning of every paragraph, and by disabling copy-paste functionality on the paragraph text."
  where: p4 [2386]

- claim: Some questions had no span answer.
  number: 2.6%
  quote: "Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers."
  where: p4 [2386]

- claim: Candidate spans were limited to constituency-parse constituents, which caps accuracy. The model finds the right sentence 79.3% of the time, so most of the difficulty is picking the exact span.
  number: 77.3% ceiling; 79.3% sentence selection
  quote: "Ignoring punctuation and articles, we find that 77.3% of the correct answers in the development set are constituents. This places an effective ceiling on the accuracy of our methods." / "the model is able to select the sentence containing the answer correctly with 79.3% accuracy; hence, the bulk of the difficulty lies in finding the exact span within the sentence."
  where: p6 [2388]; p8 [2390]

- claim: Feature ablation. Lexicalised and dependency-path features matter most. The model overfits heavily: 91.7% train F1 against 51.0% dev F1.
  number: dev F1 without both groups 35.8%; without lexicalised features 45.4%; without dependency paths 46.4%
  quote: "Logistic Regression 91.7% 51.0% / – Lex., – Dep. Paths 33.9% 35.8%" / "with lexicalized features, the model significantly overfits the training set"
  where: p8 [2390], Table 6

- claim: Span answers were chosen in part because they are easier to grade than free-form answers.
  number: none
  quote: "The span constraint also comes with the important benefit that span-based answers are easier to evaluate than free-form answers."
  where: p2 [2384]

LIMITS
- The task is extractive only, so every answer is a span of the passage. The authors grant that span questions "are more constrained than the more interpretative questions found in more advanced standardized tests" (p2).
- The 2.6% unanswerable questions are kept, and the paper does not say how they are scored.
- 6.1% of hand-labelled examples are "Ambiguous": the authors disagree with the crowd answer, or the question has no unique answer (Table 3).
- EM and F1 punish answers that are right but phrased differently from every reference. The human-mismatch quote above shows how the boundaries of non-essential words cost points.
- The human estimate rests on a single second answer. It is graded against the remaining references, so it has one fewer reference than models get. The paper does not address this asymmetry; the observation is mine.
- Every result is on v1.0. Divergence results appear only as a plot.
- Some things have dated. The paper predates SQuAD 2.0's unanswerable questions, and the 36-point gap had already halved within months. The 86.8% figure is inter-annotator agreement, not a ceiling.

BUILDS ON
- MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013): the scale comparison point and the source of the sliding-window baseline and its distance extension.
- CNN/Daily Mail cloze (Hermann et al., 2015) and CBT (Hill et al., 2015): presented as large but semi-synthetic. The paper cites Chen et al. (2016) as showing CNN/DM "requires less reasoning than previously thought."
- Earlier reading-comprehension and QA work: Hirschman et al. (1999), the TREC QA track (Voorhees and Tice, 2000), WikiQA (Yang et al., 2015) and bAbI (Weston et al., 2015).
- Crowdsourcing platform: Daemo (Gaikwad et al., 2015).
- Bigram TF-IDF weighting: Shirakawa et al. (2015).
- Motivating examples: ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) and the Penn Treebank (Marcus et al., 1993).

CODE: none in the paper. Code and data are on CodaLab (p9): https://worksheets.codalab.org/worksheets/0xd53d03a48ef64b329c16b9baf0f99b0c/

FIGURES
- Fig. 5, p8: "Performance stratified by syntactic divergence of questions and sentences. The performance of logistic regression degrades with increasing divergence. In contrast, human performance is stable across the full range of divergence." This is my pick for 03-eval-datasets. In one plot it shows that splitting results by difficulty reveals a model's brittleness, which a single average F1 hides.
- Alternatives:
  - Fig. 1, p1, sample passage with question-answer pairs: shows span answers at a glance.
  - Fig. 3, p5, worked example of the divergence edit cost.
  - Fig. 2, p3, the crowd interface: the caption fits the anti-copying point, but the image was not inspected.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean. Ligatures (fi, ff) are mangled, and the dependency-path arrows in Figs. 3–4 and Table 4 come out garbled.
- The Figure 5 data points are not in the text, so the divergence numbers could not be quoted.
- The text contains no embedded instructions.
